title: OAuth Security Best Practices
description: Learn security best practices for implementing OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect.

data.text: Implementing OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect requires careful attention to security. Following best practices ensures your application remains secure and user data is protected.
All OAuth flows must use HTTPS. Tokens, authorization codes, and user credentials are transmitted and can be intercepted over HTTP.

data.title: Critical Security Requirement
data.text: Never implement OAuth over HTTP. Use HTTPS for all endpoints, redirect URIs, and token exchanges.
Strictly validate redirect URIs to prevent open redirect attacks. Only allow pre-registered, exact-match URLs.

data.title: Redirect URI Validation

data.text: For mobile and SPA applications, use PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) to prevent authorization code interception attacks.

data.title: PKCE Implementation

data.text: Store access tokens securely. For web applications, use HTTP-only, secure cookies. For mobile apps, use the platform's secure storage.

data.title: Secure Cookie Configuration

data.text: Always use the state parameter to prevent CSRF attacks. Generate a random value, include it in the auth request, and validate it on callback.

data.title: State Parameter Implementation
data.content: Implement CSRF protection with state parameter.

data.text: Always validate ID tokens and access tokens. Check the signature, issuer, audience, and expiration.

data.title: Token Validation
data.content: Validate ID token structure and claims.

data.text: Request only the scopes you need. More scopes mean more access and higher risk if tokens are compromised.

data.title: Principle of Least Privilege
data.text: Request the minimum scopes necessary for your application to function. Don't request email access if you only need profile information.

terms.definition: Proof Key for Code Exchange - a security extension for OAuth that prevents authorization code interception.
A random value used in OAuth flows to prevent cross-site request forgery (CSRF) attacks.
Security practice of requesting only the minimum permissions needed for an application to function.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Always use HTTPS for OAuth operations
Implement state parameter for CSRF protection
data.takeaway: Following OAuth security best practices protects your application and user data from common vulnerabilities.
